subtopic: Hyperkalaemia with ECG changes: membrane stabilisation first
stem:
A 71-year-old man with stage 4 chronic kidney disease is brought to the emergency department in Wollongong, NSW, with generalised weakness for one day. He recently started spironolactone for heart failure and also takes ramipril. He is alert. His pulse is 52/min and regular and his blood pressure is 118/70 mmHg.

Investigations:
- Serum potassium 7.4 mmol/L (3.5–5.2)
- Serum creatinine 310 µmol/L (60–110)
- Venous pH 7.31

A 12-lead ECG shows tall peaked T waves, flattened P waves and a QRS duration of 150 ms. Spironolactone and ramipril are withheld.
lead_in: Which one of the following is the most appropriate immediate treatment?

options.D: Intravenous sodium bicarbonate 8.4%
options.E: Intravenous furosemide

explanation_correct: With ECG changes (peaked T waves, loss of P waves, broad QRS), the first priority is to stabilise the myocardial membrane with IV calcium (calcium gluconate 10% or calcium chloride). It acts within minutes but does not lower potassium, so it is followed straight away by insulin with glucose (with or without nebulised salbutamol) to shift potassium into cells, then measures to remove potassium (binders, dialysis). Repeat the ECG after calcium; the dose can be repeated if changes persist.

option_explanations.B: Insulin–glucose shifts potassium into cells within 15–30 minutes and should be given next, but it does not protect the heart immediately. With a broad QRS, calcium comes first.
option_explanations.C: A potassium binder lowers total body potassium over hours. Too slow for life-threatening ECG changes.
option_explanations.D: Bicarbonate has a weak, unreliable effect on potassium and is not first-line, even with mild acidosis.
option_explanations.E: A loop diuretic can increase potassium excretion when kidney function allows, but it is slow and unreliable in stage 4 CKD.

key_learning_point: Hyperkalaemia with ECG changes: IV calcium first to stabilise the myocardium, then insulin–glucose to shift potassium, then remove it.

subtopic: Suspected adrenal crisis: hydrocortisone before confirmatory testing
stem:
A 34-year-old woman is brought to a regional emergency department in Dubbo, NSW, with 3 days of vomiting, abdominal pain and dizziness. Over the past 4 months she has lost 6 kg and felt tired, and her partner says her skin has darkened even though it is winter. She has hypothyroidism treated with levothyroxine and takes no other medicines.

Her pulse is 118/min and her blood pressure is 82/50 mmHg lying. She has hyperpigmented palmar creases and buccal mucosa.

Investigations:
- Serum sodium 124 mmol/L (135–145)
- Serum potassium 5.9 mmol/L (3.5–5.2)
- Blood glucose 3.4 mmol/L
- Urea 12.1 mmol/L (2.5–8.0)

Two litres of 0.9% sodium chloride have been started. Blood has been taken for cortisol and ACTH.
lead_in: Which one of the following is the most appropriate next step?

options.A: Perform a short Synacthen (250 µg tetracosactide) test before giving steroids
options.C: Give dexamethasone 4 mg intravenously as the only steroid
options.D: Give hydrocortisone 100 mg intravenously now
options.E: Arrange an urgent CT scan of the adrenal glands

explanation_correct: This is an adrenal crisis from probable primary adrenal insufficiency (autoimmune Addison disease, with another autoimmune condition): hypotension, hyponatraemia, hyperkalaemia, hypoglycaemia and hyperpigmentation. Treatment must not wait for confirmation. Once blood for cortisol and ACTH has been taken, give hydrocortisone 100 mg IV immediately, with IV 0.9% saline and glucose, then hydrocortisone 50 mg 6-hourly (or by infusion). At this dose hydrocortisone has enough mineralocorticoid effect, so fludrocortisone is not needed acutely. The diagnosis can be confirmed later.

option_explanations.A: The Synacthen test confirms adrenal insufficiency, but delaying treatment in a crisis can be fatal. Treat first; the random cortisol and ACTH are already taken and confirmation can follow.
option_explanations.B: Fludrocortisone is long-term mineralocorticoid replacement. It is not needed acutely because high-dose hydrocortisone provides mineralocorticoid activity, and she is vomiting.
option_explanations.C: Dexamethasone has no mineralocorticoid activity and is not the preferred treatment of adrenal crisis with hyperkalaemia and hyponatraemia.
option_explanations.E: Imaging may be done later to look for a cause but has no role while she is in shock.

key_learning_point: Suspected adrenal crisis: take blood for cortisol/ACTH, then give IV hydrocortisone 100 mg immediately. Never delay for a Synacthen test.

subtopic: Screening for Cushing syndrome in a woman taking the combined oral contraceptive pill
stem:
A 29-year-old woman sees her general practitioner in Hobart, Tasmania, because she has gained 14 kg over 18 months. She has new purple abdominal striae up to 1.5 cm wide, easy bruising and difficulty climbing stairs. She has taken a combined oral contraceptive pill containing ethinylestradiol for 8 years. She uses no topical, inhaled or oral glucocorticoids.

Her blood pressure is 154/96 mmHg and BMI 33 kg/m². She has facial plethora and proximal muscle weakness. Her HbA1c is 6.6%.

The GP suspects Cushing syndrome. She does not want to stop her pill.
lead_in: Which one of the following is the most appropriate initial investigation?

options.D: Late-night salivary cortisol measured on two separate nights
options.E: High-dose (8 mg) dexamethasone suppression test

explanation_correct: Wide purple striae, easy bruising, proximal myopathy, plethora, new hypertension and dysglycaemia make Cushing syndrome a real possibility. First-line screening tests are the overnight 1 mg dexamethasone suppression test, late-night salivary cortisol (at least two) or 24-hour urinary free cortisol (at least two). Oral oestrogen raises cortisol-binding globulin, which raises total serum cortisol and causes false-positive dexamethasone suppression tests in a large proportion of women. Salivary cortisol measures free cortisol, is not affected by CBG, and is the best choice when she will not stop the pill (ideally the pill is stopped for about 6 weeks before a DST).

option_explanations.A: Valid in most people, but oral oestrogen raises CBG and total serum cortisol, so false positives are common in women on the combined pill.
option_explanations.B: A single serum cortisol cannot separate Cushing syndrome from normal, because of diurnal variation and stress. It is not a screening test.
option_explanations.C: ACTH is used after hypercortisolism is confirmed, to separate ACTH-dependent from ACTH-independent causes.
option_explanations.E: This was used to localise the source in confirmed ACTH-dependent disease. It has no role in initial screening.

key_learning_point: Screen for Cushing syndrome with late-night salivary cortisol, 24-hour UFC or a 1 mg DST. Oral oestrogen causes false-positive DSTs by raising CBG.

subtopic: Cholestatic liver tests with normal ducts in a middle-aged woman: antimitochondrial antibody
stem:
A 52-year-old woman sees her general practitioner in Toowoomba, Queensland, with 6 months of itch, worse at night, and tiredness. She has no rash, takes no medicines or supplements and rarely drinks alcohol. She has no inflammatory bowel disease. Examination shows excoriations but no jaundice or signs of chronic liver disease.

Investigations:
- ALP 412 U/L (30–110)
- GGT 380 U/L (<38)
- ALT 58 U/L (<35)
- Bilirubin 15 µmol/L (<20)
- Albumin 39 g/L (35–50)

Abdominal ultrasound shows normal liver texture, a normal gallbladder and no intrahepatic or extrahepatic bile duct dilatation.
lead_in: Which one of the following tests is most likely to confirm the diagnosis?

options.D: Liver biopsy
options.E: Serum antimitochondrial antibody

explanation_correct: Pruritus and fatigue with a cholestatic pattern (ALP and GGT raised far more than ALT) and non-dilated ducts in a middle-aged woman suggests primary biliary cholangitis. A positive antimitochondrial antibody (M2) with a raised ALP is diagnostic in most cases without liver biopsy. Treatment is ursodeoxycholic acid.

option_explanations.A: This supports autoimmune hepatitis, which gives a mainly hepatocellular (ALT-predominant) pattern.
option_explanations.B: MRCP is the test for primary sclerosing cholangitis, typically in younger men with IBD. It is used if the AMA is negative.
option_explanations.C: Ceruloplasmin is a test for Wilson disease, which usually presents before age 40 with hepatic or neuropsychiatric features.
option_explanations.D: Biopsy is rarely needed for PBC. It is kept for AMA-negative cases or suspected overlap with autoimmune hepatitis.

key_learning_point: Middle-aged woman, itch, cholestatic LFTs, normal ducts on ultrasound: test AMA for primary biliary cholangitis.

subtopic: Raised ferritin: transferrin saturation separates iron overload from a metabolic cause
stem:
Two men see the same general practitioner in Bendigo, Victoria, about a raised ferritin found on routine blood tests. Neither has symptoms, and both drink fewer than 10 standard drinks a week.

Man 1 is 46, with a BMI of 33 kg/m², type 2 diabetes and fatty liver on ultrasound.
Man 2 is 44, with a BMI of 24 kg/m²; his father had 'liver trouble'.

Investigations (fasting):
| | Man 1 | Man 2 |
|---|---|---|
| Ferritin (30–500 µg/L) | 780 | 760 |
| Transferrin saturation (15–45%) | 28 | 71 |
| ALT (<40 U/L) | 64 | 52 |
| CRP (<5 mg/L) | 6 | 2 |
lead_in: Which one of the following is the most appropriate interpretation?

options.A: Both men most likely have haemochromatosis and should have HFE genotyping
options.B: Man 1 most likely has haemochromatosis because he has diabetes and a raised ALT
options.C: Man 2 most likely has HFE haemochromatosis and should have HFE genotyping
options.D: Neither man needs further testing because their ferritin is below 1000 µg/L
options.E: Both men should start venesection now and then be genotyped

explanation_correct: Ferritin rises with iron overload but also with inflammation, alcohol, fatty liver and metabolic syndrome. Transferrin saturation separates these. A fasting transferrin saturation above 45% with a raised ferritin suggests iron overload, and HFE genotyping (C282Y, H63D) is the next step; Man 2 fits, with a possible family history. Man 1 has a normal transferrin saturation, so his ferritin most likely reflects metabolic dysfunction-associated fatty liver disease (dysmetabolic hyperferritinaemia). He does not need HFE testing or venesection; he needs management of weight and metabolic risk.

option_explanations.A: A ferritin above 500 µg/L alone does not mean iron overload. Man 1's normal transferrin saturation points away from haemochromatosis.
option_explanations.B: Diabetes and a raised ALT are better explained by fatty liver; his transferrin saturation is normal.
option_explanations.D: Ferritin below 1000 µg/L lowers the risk of advanced fibrosis in haemochromatosis but does not exclude it. Man 2 still needs genotyping.
option_explanations.E: Venesection follows a diagnosis of iron overload. Man 1 has no evidence of iron overload.

key_learning_point: Raised ferritin: check fasting transferrin saturation. TSAT >45% suggests iron overload (HFE genotyping); normal TSAT points to inflammation, alcohol or fatty liver.

subtopic: Cellulitis with a non-severe delayed penicillin rash: oral cefalexin
stem:
A 58-year-old man sees his general practitioner in Mandurah, Western Australia, with 2 days of spreading redness and pain over his left shin after a gardening scratch. He feels well. He has type 2 diabetes treated with metformin. As a child he developed a mild itchy rash 4 days into a course of amoxicillin; it settled without treatment, with no blistering, mucosal involvement or organ involvement. He has had no penicillins since.

His temperature is 37.8 °C, pulse 84/min and blood pressure 134/82 mmHg. There is a 10 × 8 cm area of warm, tender, non-fluctuant erythema on the shin, with no crepitus or bullae, and pain in proportion to the signs. He has interdigital tinea of the left foot.
lead_in: Which one of the following is the most appropriate antibiotic?

options.D: Intravenous cefazolin in hospital
options.E: Oral cefalexin

explanation_correct: This is non-purulent cellulitis without systemic toxicity, suitable for oral treatment. First-line therapy targets streptococci and Staphylococcus aureus (flucloxacillin or cefalexin). His past reaction was a mild, delayed, non-severe rash; eTG advises that patients with a non-severe delayed penicillin reaction can usually be given a cephalosporin such as cefalexin. Clindamycin (or trimethoprim–sulfamethoxazole) is kept for immediate (IgE-mediated) or severe delayed reactions. The tinea should be treated as a portal of entry, the leg elevated, and penicillin allergy delabelling considered later.

option_explanations.A: Clindamycin is for immediate or severe penicillin hypersensitivity; it has more adverse effects, including C. difficile infection.
option_explanations.B: First-line without allergy, but with a documented penicillin reaction a cephalosporin is used for a non-severe delayed reaction unless he has been formally delabelled.
option_explanations.C: This is a penicillin and gives broader cover than cellulitis needs; it is used for bites and some diabetic foot infections.
option_explanations.D: He has no systemic toxicity, rapid spread or high-risk features, so oral treatment in the community is appropriate.

key_learning_point: Cellulitis with a past mild delayed penicillin rash: oral cefalexin. Reserve clindamycin for immediate or severe reactions.

subtopic: Löfgren syndrome: clinical diagnosis without tissue biopsy
stem:
A 31-year-old woman who moved from Sweden to Perth 2 years ago sees her general practitioner with 10 days of fever, painful swollen ankles and tender red lumps on both shins. She has no cough, weight loss or night sweats, no recent travel and no known tuberculosis contacts. She takes no medicines.

Her temperature is 37.9 °C. Both ankles are swollen with periarticular tenderness. There are several tender, raised, red-purple nodules 2–4 cm across on both anterior shins. Chest examination is normal, with no peripheral lymphadenopathy or hepatosplenomegaly.

Investigations:
- CRP 48 mg/L (<5)
- Corrected calcium 2.48 mmol/L (2.10–2.60)
- Chest X-ray: bilateral symmetrical hilar lymphadenopathy; clear lung fields
- Interferon-gamma release assay negative
lead_in: Which one of the following is the most appropriate interpretation?

options.A: Lymphoma; she needs an urgent biopsy of a mediastinal node
options.B: Primary tuberculosis; she should start four-drug treatment
options.C: Chronic pulmonary sarcoidosis needing high-dose oral prednisolone
options.D: Löfgren syndrome (acute sarcoidosis); a biopsy is not needed and the outlook is good
options.E: Reactive arthritis after a gastrointestinal infection

explanation_correct: Erythema nodosum, bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy, fever and ankle periarthritis is the classic picture of Löfgren syndrome, an acute form of sarcoidosis that is more common in women of Scandinavian descent. When the presentation is typical and there are no atypical features (weight loss, asymmetric or bulky nodes, a positive TB test), the combination is specific enough that biopsy is generally not needed. Most cases resolve spontaneously within 1–2 years. Treatment is supportive with NSAIDs; corticosteroids are rarely needed. A repeat chest X-ray confirms resolution.

option_explanations.A: Lymphoma rarely causes this acute triad and usually gives asymmetric or bulky nodes and B symptoms.
option_explanations.B: She has no TB contacts, no respiratory symptoms and a negative IGRA. The full picture favours Löfgren syndrome.
option_explanations.C: Löfgren syndrome is acute and self-limiting with clear lungs; steroids are not routinely needed.
option_explanations.E: Reactive arthritis does not cause hilar lymphadenopathy, and there was no preceding diarrhoea or urethritis.

key_learning_point: Erythema nodosum + bilateral hilar nodes + fever + ankle periarthritis = Löfgren syndrome. A typical case needs no biopsy; NSAIDs and follow-up.

subtopic: Suspected idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis: high-resolution CT
stem:
A 69-year-old retired carpenter sees his general practitioner in Launceston, Tasmania, with 9 months of gradually worsening exertional breathlessness and a dry cough. He smoked 20 cigarettes a day for 25 years and stopped 15 years ago. He has no joint symptoms, rash, pets or birds, and takes no regular medicines.

His SpO2 is 95% at rest on room air. He has digital clubbing and fine 'velcro-like' inspiratory crackles at both lung bases. There is no ankle oedema.

Investigations:
- Spirometry: FEV1 78% predicted, FVC 70% predicted, FEV1/FVC 0.84
- DLCO 52% predicted
- Chest X-ray: reticular shadowing at both bases
lead_in: Which one of the following is the most appropriate next investigation?

options.C: High-resolution CT scan of the chest
options.D: Bronchoscopy with bronchoalveolar lavage
options.E: Repeat spirometry after a bronchodilator

explanation_correct: Progressive exertional breathlessness, dry cough, clubbing, bibasal velcro crackles, a restrictive pattern (preserved FEV1/FVC with reduced FVC) and a low DLCO strongly suggest interstitial lung disease, most likely idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis in an older male ex-smoker. HRCT is the key investigation: a usual interstitial pneumonia pattern (subpleural basal reticulation, honeycombing, traction bronchiectasis) in the right clinical context, after excluding other causes, allows diagnosis without biopsy. He should be referred to a respiratory physician for multidisciplinary discussion and consideration of antifibrotic therapy.

option_explanations.A: Biopsy is reserved for when HRCT and multidisciplinary review are not diagnostic; it carries real risk in IPF.
option_explanations.B: CTPA looks for pulmonary embolism, which does not explain months of progressive symptoms, crackles, clubbing and restriction.
option_explanations.D: BAL can help in some ILDs (such as hypersensitivity pneumonitis) but HRCT comes first.
option_explanations.E: Bronchodilator testing looks for reversible obstruction; his pattern is restrictive.

key_learning_point: Velcro crackles, clubbing, restriction and low DLCO suggest pulmonary fibrosis: arrange HRCT chest. A typical UIP pattern may avoid biopsy.

subtopic: Systolic murmur in a young athlete: dynamic manoeuvre for hypertrophic cardiomyopathy
stem:
A 19-year-old university footballer sees a sports physician in Adelaide after feeling lightheaded during a sprint at training last week. He did not lose consciousness. His uncle died suddenly aged 32. He takes no medicines or supplements.

His pulse is 64/min and regular and blood pressure 122/74 mmHg. He has a grade 3/6 harsh ejection systolic murmur, loudest at the left lower sternal edge, that does not radiate to the carotids. His carotid pulse is brisk. An echocardiogram will be arranged, but the physician first examines the murmur further at the bedside.
lead_in: Which one of the following findings would most support the likely diagnosis?

options.A: The murmur becomes louder when he squats from standing
options.B: The murmur becomes louder during the strain phase of a Valsalva manoeuvre
options.C: The murmur becomes louder with sustained isometric handgrip
options.D: The murmur radiates to both carotids with a slow-rising pulse
options.E: The murmur becomes softer when he stands up from squatting

explanation_correct: Exertional presyncope, a family history of sudden death and a harsh systolic murmur at the left sternal edge with a brisk carotid pulse suggest hypertrophic cardiomyopathy with left ventricular outflow tract obstruction. The obstruction is dynamic: reducing preload (Valsalva strain, standing from squatting) makes the ventricle smaller and the murmur louder; increasing preload or afterload (squatting, passive leg raise, handgrip) makes it softer. This is the opposite of aortic stenosis. He should stop competitive sport until assessed and have an echocardiogram, ECG and cardiology review.

option_explanations.A: Squatting increases venous return and afterload, reducing obstruction, so the HCM murmur softens.
option_explanations.C: Handgrip raises afterload, which reduces the outflow gradient; it makes mitral regurgitation louder, not HCM.
option_explanations.D: A slow-rising pulse with carotid radiation suggests aortic stenosis. HCM gives a brisk, sometimes bifid, pulse.
option_explanations.E: Standing suddenly reduces preload and worsens obstruction, so the HCM murmur gets louder.

key_learning_point: HCM murmur: louder with less preload (Valsalva strain, standing), softer with more preload or afterload (squatting, handgrip). Opposite to aortic stenosis.

subtopic: Pleuritic chest pain with widespread ST elevation and PR depression: acute pericarditis
stem:
A 26-year-old man presents to an emergency department in Canberra with 2 days of sharp central chest pain, worse lying flat and on deep breathing, and eased by sitting forward. He had a sore throat and runny nose a week ago. He has no past medical history.

His temperature is 37.6 °C, pulse 96/min and blood pressure 126/78 mmHg. A scratchy sound is heard at the left sternal edge with him leaning forward. His chest is clear.

The ECG shows concave ST elevation in I, II, aVL, aVF and V2–V6, with PR depression in the same leads and PR elevation in aVR, and no reciprocal ST depression. High-sensitivity troponin is normal on two samples.
lead_in: Which one of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

options.D: Pulmonary embolism
options.E: Benign early repolarisation

explanation_correct: Pleuritic, positional chest pain relieved by sitting forward, a friction rub, a preceding viral illness and widespread concave ST elevation with PR depression (PR elevation in aVR) without reciprocal change is typical of acute pericarditis. A normal troponin makes significant myocardial involvement unlikely. An echocardiogram looks for an effusion. First-line treatment is an NSAID (or aspirin) plus colchicine for 3 months, which reduces recurrence.

option_explanations.A: STEMI gives convex ST elevation in a coronary territory with reciprocal depression and rising troponin.
option_explanations.C: Myocarditis would usually raise troponin and may impair ventricular function.
option_explanations.D: PE can cause pleuritic pain and tachycardia but not a rub, positional relief or diffuse ST elevation with PR depression.
option_explanations.E: Early repolarisation occurs without symptoms, rub or PR depression, and does not evolve.

key_learning_point: Pleuritic pain eased by sitting forward + rub + diffuse saddle ST elevation with PR depression = acute pericarditis. NSAID plus colchicine.

subtopic: Lower motor neurone facial palsy with ear vesicles: Ramsay Hunt syndrome
stem:
A 63-year-old man sees his general practitioner in Cairns, Queensland, because the right side of his face has drooped since he woke this morning. For 3 days he has had severe burning pain deep in his right ear. Food tastes strange and loud sounds are uncomfortable in his right ear. He has type 2 diabetes.

He cannot wrinkle his right forehead, close his right eye fully or raise the right corner of his mouth. There are small clustered vesicles on an erythematous base in the right external auditory canal and concha. The rest of the neurological examination is normal.
lead_in: Which one of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

options.D: Acute otitis media with facial nerve involvement
options.E: Parotid gland tumour

explanation_correct: A lower motor neurone facial palsy (forehead involved) with ear pain and vesicles in the canal and concha is Ramsay Hunt syndrome, from varicella-zoster reactivation in the geniculate ganglion. Altered taste and hyperacusis reflect chorda tympani and stapedius nerve involvement. Compared with Bell palsy it is more painful, more often complete, and has a poorer chance of full recovery; it may also cause hearing loss or vertigo. Treatment is prednisolone plus an antiviral (such as valaciclovir) started early, with eye protection.

option_explanations.B: Bell palsy is a diagnosis of exclusion; the vesicles indicate VZV, which changes treatment (antiviral) and prognosis.
option_explanations.C: Stroke causes upper motor neurone facial weakness that spares the forehead, usually with other signs.
option_explanations.D: Otitis media affects the middle ear (bulging drum) and does not cause canal or concha vesicles.
option_explanations.E: A parotid malignancy causes gradual palsy with a parotid mass, not vesicles.

key_learning_point: Facial palsy (forehead involved) + ear pain + vesicles in the canal or concha = Ramsay Hunt syndrome. Prednisolone plus antiviral early.

subtopic: Headache with papilloedema in a young woman: MRI with MR venography before lumbar puncture
stem:
A 27-year-old woman presents to an emergency department in Newcastle, NSW, with 6 weeks of daily headache, worse lying down and on waking, and brief episodes of her vision 'greying out' when she stands. She hears a pulsing 'whooshing' sound in both ears. She started the combined oral contraceptive pill 4 months ago and has gained 8 kg in the past year. Her BMI is 36 kg/m².

She is afebrile and her blood pressure is 124/80 mmHg. Fundoscopy shows bilateral optic disc swelling. Visual acuity is 6/6 in both eyes. She has a mild right sixth nerve palsy; the rest of the neurological examination is normal. A non-contrast CT brain is normal.
lead_in: Which one of the following is the most appropriate next investigation?

options.D: Formal visual field testing alone with GP follow-up
options.E: Carotid duplex ultrasound

explanation_correct: Headache with papilloedema means raised intracranial pressure. Idiopathic intracranial hypertension is likely in an obese young woman (a sixth nerve palsy is a non-localising sign), but it is a diagnosis of exclusion. Cerebral venous sinus thrombosis can look identical, and she has a prothrombotic risk factor (the combined pill). A non-contrast CT can miss venous sinus thrombosis. MRI with MR venography (or CT venography) should come before lumbar puncture. If imaging is normal, LP with opening pressure (lateral decubitus) and CSF analysis confirms IIH. She also needs formal visual fields and ophthalmology review.

option_explanations.A: LP confirms IIH only after imaging has excluded a mass and venous sinus thrombosis; a normal non-contrast CT is not enough.
option_explanations.B: These look for giant cell arteritis in people over 50; they do not help here.
option_explanations.D: Fields are essential for monitoring, but they do not exclude secondary causes; she needs urgent venous imaging.
option_explanations.E: Carotid disease does not cause papilloedema or a raised-pressure headache.

key_learning_point: Papilloedema with a normal CT: MRI with MR venography to exclude venous sinus thrombosis before LP. IIH is a diagnosis of exclusion.

subtopic: Raised haemoglobin with aquagenic itch and splenomegaly: JAK2 V617F with low EPO confirms polycythaemia vera
stem:
A 61-year-old man sees his general practitioner in Geelong, Victoria, with 3 months of headaches and intense itch after hot showers. He has never smoked, does not snore and takes no medicines, including testosterone. SpO2 is 98% on room air. He has a ruddy complexion and the spleen tip is palpable 2 cm below the costal margin.

Investigations:
- Haemoglobin 198 g/L (130–180)
- Haematocrit 0.59 (0.40–0.52)
- White cell count 13.1 × 10^9/L (4.0–11.0)
- Platelets 520 × 10^9/L (150–400)
lead_in: Which one of the following results would most strongly confirm the likely diagnosis?

options.A: Raised serum erythropoietin with a normal JAK2 result
options.B: JAK2 V617F mutation detected, with a low serum erythropoietin
options.D: Raised ferritin with a raised transferrin saturation
options.E: Low saturation on overnight oximetry

explanation_correct: Raised haemoglobin and haematocrit with leucocytosis, thrombocytosis, splenomegaly and aquagenic pruritus, without hypoxia, smoking or testosterone, strongly suggests polycythaemia vera. A JAK2 mutation (V617F or exon 12) is present in about 95% of cases and is a major WHO criterion; a low serum EPO is the minor criterion and reflects EPO-independent erythropoiesis (secondary polycythaemia has normal or high EPO). Management is haematology referral, venesection to a haematocrit below 0.45 and low-dose aspirin, with cytoreduction for high-risk patients.

option_explanations.A: This suggests secondary polycythaemia (hypoxia, renal tumour), not PV.
option_explanations.C: BCR-ABL1 defines chronic myeloid leukaemia, which does not raise haemoglobin.
option_explanations.D: This suggests iron overload; PV patients are often iron deficient.
option_explanations.E: Nocturnal hypoxia causes secondary polycythaemia, arguing against PV.

key_learning_point: Raised Hb + splenomegaly + aquagenic itch (± high WCC/platelets): JAK2 V617F with low EPO = polycythaemia vera.

subtopic: Polymyalgia rheumatica without features of giant cell arteritis: prednisolone 15 mg daily
stem:
A 72-year-old woman sees her general practitioner in Albury, NSW, with 5 weeks of aching and stiffness of both shoulders and hips. The stiffness lasts about 2 hours each morning and she struggles to get out of bed and comb her hair. She has no headache, scalp tenderness, jaw pain on chewing or visual symptoms, and no weight loss, joint swelling or rash.

Active shoulder movement is limited by pain, but strength is normal. Her temporal arteries are non-tender with normal pulses. There is no synovitis.

Investigations:
- ESR 64 mm/h (<30)
- CRP 42 mg/L (<5)
- Creatine kinase normal
- Rheumatoid factor and anti-CCP negative
- FBC, calcium, TSH, electrolytes and LFTs normal
lead_in: Which one of the following is the most appropriate management?

options.A: Oral prednisolone 15 mg daily, with review of the response in 1–2 weeks
options.B: Oral prednisolone 60 mg daily and urgent temporal artery biopsy
options.C: Regular oral NSAIDs and review in 4 weeks
options.D: Methotrexate as first-line monotherapy
options.E: Intramuscular methylprednisolone 120 mg weekly

explanation_correct: Bilateral shoulder and hip girdle aching with prolonged morning stiffness, raised inflammatory markers, a normal CK and no features of another rheumatic disease or giant cell arteritis fits polymyalgia rheumatica. Treatment is oral prednisolone 12.5–25 mg daily (commonly 15 mg). A rapid, marked response supports the diagnosis; a poor response should prompt a search for another cause. The dose is tapered slowly over 1–2 years. Consider bone protection, and tell her to report GCA symptoms urgently.

option_explanations.B: This dose is for suspected giant cell arteritis; she has no headache, jaw claudication, scalp tenderness or visual symptoms.
option_explanations.C: NSAIDs give little benefit in PMR, carry more risk in older people and delay effective treatment.
option_explanations.D: Methotrexate is a steroid-sparing add-on for relapsing disease or high steroid risk, not first-line monotherapy.
option_explanations.E: IM methylprednisolone is an alternative in some guidelines, but not as a weekly regimen; oral prednisolone is standard.

key_learning_point: PMR without GCA features: prednisolone 12.5–25 mg daily (often 15 mg). Expect a dramatic response; if not, reconsider the diagnosis.

subtopic: High anion gap acidosis with a raised osmolar gap and oxalate crystals: ethylene glycol
stem:
A 45-year-old man is brought to an emergency department in Ipswich, Queensland, by his housemate, who found him confused and vomiting in the garage near empty containers. He has alcohol use disorder. He is drowsy but rousable, with no focal neurological signs; pupils and fundi are normal. Pulse is 112/min, blood pressure 138/84 mmHg and respiratory rate 30/min.

Investigations:
- Venous pH 7.08; bicarbonate 7 mmol/L
- Sodium 140 mmol/L; chloride 101 mmol/L; potassium 5.0 mmol/L
- Glucose 5.0 mmol/L; urea 6.0 mmol/L
- Creatinine 190 µmol/L (60–110)
- Lactate 2.6 mmol/L (<2.0)
- Measured serum osmolality 335 mOsm/kg
- Blood ethanol undetectable
- Urine microscopy: many envelope-shaped and needle-shaped crystals
lead_in: Which one of the following is the most likely cause of his presentation?

options.D: Salicylate poisoning
options.E: Ethylene glycol poisoning

explanation_correct: Anion gap = Na − (Cl + HCO3) = 140 − (101 + 7) = 32 mmol/L, very high and not explained by a lactate of 2.6. Calculated osmolality = 2 × Na + glucose + urea = 280 + 5 + 6 = 291, so the osmolar gap is 335 − 291 = 44 mOsm/kg (normal below about 10) with no ethanol to explain it. A high anion gap acidosis with a high osmolar gap means a toxic alcohol. Calcium oxalate crystals (envelope-shaped dihydrate, needle-shaped monohydrate) and acute kidney injury point to ethylene glycol (antifreeze, coolant). Treatment is fomepizole (or ethanol) to block alcohol dehydrogenase, haemodialysis and correction of acidosis, with advice from the Poisons Information Centre (13 11 26).

option_explanations.A: Methanol also raises both gaps, but typically causes visual symptoms and disc changes, not oxalate crystals and prominent AKI.
option_explanations.B: AKA causes a high anion gap acidosis but not a large osmolar gap, oxalate crystals or this degree of AKI.
option_explanations.C: Isopropyl alcohol raises the osmolar gap but is metabolised to acetone, causing ketosis without significant acidosis.
option_explanations.D: Salicylates cause a high anion gap acidosis, often with respiratory alkalosis and tinnitus, but not a large osmolar gap or oxalate crystals.

key_learning_point: High anion gap acidosis + high osmolar gap = toxic alcohol. Oxalate crystals + AKI = ethylene glycol; visual disturbance = methanol. Fomepizole and dialysis.

subtopic: Acute limb ischaemia with a salvageable limb in atrial fibrillation: heparin and urgent vascular review
stem:
A 76-year-old woman presents to an emergency department in Rockhampton, Queensland, 3 hours after the sudden onset of pain and numbness in her right leg while watching television. She has atrial fibrillation but stopped her apixaban 2 months ago because of bruising. She has no history of claudication.

Her pulse is 104/min and irregularly irregular, blood pressure 150/88 mmHg. The right leg is pale and cool from mid-calf down. The right femoral pulse is present but the popliteal and foot pulses are absent. Light touch is mildly reduced over the toes; toe movement is normal. The left leg has normal pulses. Handheld Doppler signals are absent in the right foot arteries but present in the veins.
lead_in: Which one of the following is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.A: Restart apixaban and arrange an outpatient arterial duplex scan
options.B: Give aspirin 300 mg and arrange vascular review the next morning
options.D: Give an intravenous bolus of unfractionated heparin and arrange urgent vascular surgical review
options.E: Elevate the leg and apply a warm blanket

explanation_correct: Sudden onset of a cold, painful, pulseless leg in a woman with AF off anticoagulation, normal contralateral pulses and no claudication history is acute embolic limb ischaemia (probably popliteal). Mild sensory loss with preserved movement and audible venous but not arterial Doppler signals is Rutherford IIa (marginally threatened). Immediate treatment is an IV unfractionated heparin bolus then infusion to stop clot propagation, analgesia, and urgent vascular surgery for revascularisation (embolectomy or catheter-directed therapy) within hours.

option_explanations.A: Acute limb ischaemia is a surgical emergency; delay risks limb loss.
option_explanations.B: Aspirin does not stop clot propagation adequately, and waiting risks irreversible ischaemia.
option_explanations.C: Amputation is for an irreversible (class III) limb with profound sensory loss, paralysis and no arterial or venous Doppler signals.
option_explanations.E: Elevation reduces perfusion pressure and warming increases metabolic demand; keep the leg level or slightly dependent.

key_learning_point: Acute limb ischaemia with a salvageable limb: IV heparin bolus, analgesia and urgent vascular surgery for revascularisation.

subtopic: Perianal abscess: incision and drainage
stem:
A 38-year-old man sees his general practitioner in Bunbury, Western Australia, with 4 days of worsening constant throbbing pain beside his anus; sitting is painful. He has had no change in bowel habit or rectal bleeding, and has no inflammatory bowel disease, diabetes or immune compromise.

His temperature is 37.9 °C. There is a 3 cm tender, red, fluctuant swelling 2 cm from the anal verge at the 4 o'clock position. Digital rectal examination is too painful to complete.
lead_in: Which one of the following is the most appropriate management?

options.A: Oral amoxicillin–clavulanate and review in 1 week
options.B: Sitz baths, stool softeners and topical glyceryl trinitrate
options.D: Same-day referral for incision and drainage
options.E: Elective colonoscopy

explanation_correct: A tender fluctuant perianal swelling with fever is a perianal abscess. Definitive treatment is prompt surgical incision and drainage, usually under anaesthesia so that examination under anaesthesia can also look for a fistula. Antibiotics alone do not cure an established abscess; they are added for spreading cellulitis, systemic sepsis, diabetes or immune compromise. Delay risks spread to deeper spaces.

option_explanations.A: Antibiotics alone do not treat an established collection, and the abscess may spread.
option_explanations.B: This treats an anal fissure (sharp pain on defecation, posterior midline tear), not a fluctuant mass.
option_explanations.C: Banding is for internal haemorrhoids; it does not treat infection.
option_explanations.E: Colonoscopy may be needed later if Crohn disease is suspected but does not treat the abscess.

key_learning_point: Perianal abscess: urgent incision and drainage. Antibiotics alone are not enough.

subtopic: Suspected first episode of acute diverticulitis: contrast CT to confirm and stage
stem:
A 64-year-old man presents to an emergency department in Ballarat, Victoria, with 2 days of constant left iliac fossa pain and loose stools. He has never had a colonoscopy; his last screening iFOBT 4 years ago was negative.

His temperature is 38.1 °C, pulse 98/min and blood pressure 132/80 mmHg. There is localised left iliac fossa tenderness and guarding, without generalised peritonism. Bowel sounds are present.

Investigations:
- White cell count 14.2 × 10^9/L (4.0–11.0)
- CRP 128 mg/L (<5)
- Creatinine and liver function normal
lead_in: Which one of the following is the most appropriate investigation to confirm the diagnosis?

options.C: CT scan of the abdomen and pelvis with intravenous contrast
options.D: Barium enema
options.E: Faecal calprotectin

explanation_correct: Left iliac fossa pain, fever and raised inflammatory markers in an older adult suggest acute diverticulitis. With no previous episode, imaging is needed to confirm it, to separate uncomplicated from complicated disease (abscess, perforation, fistula, obstruction) and to exclude other causes; contrast CT is preferred. Uncomplicated disease in a well, immunocompetent patient may be managed without antibiotics; an abscess may need drainage. Colonoscopy is usually done 6–8 weeks after recovery to exclude cancer if the colon has not been recently assessed.

option_explanations.A: Colonoscopy in acute diverticulitis risks perforation and is deferred for about 6–8 weeks.
option_explanations.B: A plain film may show free gas or obstruction but cannot diagnose or stage diverticulitis.
option_explanations.D: Contrast enema has no acute role, and barium can cause severe peritonitis if perforated.
option_explanations.E: Calprotectin helps separate IBD from functional disorders; it does not confirm diverticulitis or its complications.

key_learning_point: Suspected first diverticulitis: CT abdomen/pelvis with IV contrast. Defer colonoscopy for 6–8 weeks.

subtopic: Large bowel obstruction in an older institutionalised man: sigmoid volvulus on plain X-ray
stem:
An 82-year-old man from a residential aged care facility in Mildura, Victoria, is brought to the emergency department with 2 days of increasing abdominal distension, colicky pain and no passage of stool or flatus. He has Parkinson disease and chronic constipation, and takes regular opioids for back pain.

He is afebrile, pulse 96/min, blood pressure 128/76 mmHg. His abdomen is grossly distended and tympanic, with mild generalised tenderness but no guarding. Bowel sounds are high-pitched. The rectum is empty.

A supine abdominal X-ray shows a hugely dilated inverted-U loop of large bowel without haustra ('coffee bean'), arising from the left lower quadrant and pointing to the right upper quadrant. There is no free gas on the erect chest X-ray.
lead_in: Which one of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

options.D: Obstructing sigmoid carcinoma
options.E: Adhesive small bowel obstruction

explanation_correct: An older institutionalised man with neurological disease, chronic constipation and opioid use is the typical patient. The 'coffee bean' (bent inner tube) sign, a hugely dilated haustra-free loop arising from the pelvis and pointing towards the right upper quadrant, is characteristic; CT can confirm it (whirl sign). Without ischaemia or perforation, initial treatment is endoscopic decompression (flexible sigmoidoscopy) with a flatus tube. Recurrence is common, so elective sigmoid colectomy during the same admission is usually advised if he is fit.

option_explanations.A: Caecal volvulus gives a dilated loop in the left upper quadrant with small bowel dilatation, usually in younger patients.
option_explanations.C: Pseudo-obstruction shows diffuse colonic dilatation (often caecal), not a single twisted loop.
option_explanations.D: A tumour causes proximal colonic dilatation with preserved haustra, not a single haustra-free twisted loop.
option_explanations.E: Small bowel loops are central with valvulae conniventes; this is a large bowel loop and he has no surgical history.

key_learning_point: 'Coffee bean' loop from pelvis to RUQ in an older constipated patient = sigmoid volvulus. Endoscopic decompression if no ischaemia, then consider colectomy.

subtopic: Suspected scaphoid fracture with a normal initial X-ray: immobilise and re-image
stem:
A 22-year-old right-handed man sees his general practitioner in Mackay, Queensland, the day after falling onto his outstretched right hand while skateboarding. He has pain on the radial side of the wrist.

There is mild swelling and marked tenderness in the anatomical snuffbox, and pain on axial compression of the thumb. There is no deformity and the hand is neurovascularly intact.

Wrist X-rays, including dedicated scaphoid views, show no fracture.
lead_in: Which one of the following is the most appropriate next step?

options.A: Immobilise the wrist in a splint and arrange further scaphoid imaging
options.B: Reassure him that it is a sprain and apply a compression bandage
options.C: Refer for urgent open reduction and internal fixation
options.D: Arrange a wrist ultrasound
options.E: Start range-of-motion exercises and review if pain persists at 6 weeks

explanation_correct: Snuffbox tenderness and pain on axial thumb loading after a fall on the outstretched hand mean a scaphoid fracture must be presumed even when first X-rays are normal; about 20% of clinically suspected fractures with normal initial films are true fractures. Because the proximal pole's blood supply is retrograde, a missed waist fracture risks non-union and avascular necrosis. Immobilise the wrist (a short-arm cast or splint is as effective as a thumb spica) and arrange early review with further imaging: repeat scaphoid X-rays at about 10–14 days in fracture clinic, with MRI if tenderness persists and the repeat film is normal, or early MRI/CT where available. A confirmed fracture is immobilised for about 6 weeks.

option_explanations.B: A normal first X-ray does not exclude a scaphoid fracture; missing one risks non-union and AVN.
option_explanations.C: Surgery is for confirmed displaced or proximal pole fractures; none is confirmed yet.
option_explanations.D: Ultrasound is not reliable for occult scaphoid fracture.
option_explanations.E: Mobilising an unrecognised fracture increases the risk of non-union.

key_learning_point: Snuffbox tenderness with a normal X-ray: treat as a scaphoid fracture. Immobilise and re-image (MRI/CT, or repeat X-ray at 10–14 days).

references.name: Royal Children's Hospital. Scaphoid fractures – emergency management (clinical practice guideline)

reviewer_notes: Key wording now matches the RCH scaphoid guideline (read live 7 Oct 2026): immobilise, repeat X-ray at fracture clinic in 1–2 weeks, MRI if tenderness persists. RCH is a paediatric/adolescent guideline; no adult Australian ED guideline was read, so the flag stays for an adult-source check.

subtopic: Ottawa ankle rules: which finding mandates an ankle X-ray
stem:
A 34-year-old woman presents to an emergency department in Darwin, Northern Territory, 2 hours after rolling her right ankle inwards stepping off a kerb. She has pain over the outside of the ankle.

There is swelling and bruising below and in front of the lateral malleolus. The doctor applies the Ottawa ankle rules to decide whether she needs an X-ray.
lead_in: Which one of the following findings would indicate that an ankle X-ray is needed?

options.A: Swelling and bruising over the lateral ankle
options.B: Tenderness over the anterior talofibular ligament
options.C: Pain when walking, although she can take four steps
options.D: Age over 30 years
options.E: Bone tenderness at the posterior edge of the distal 6 cm of the lateral malleolus

explanation_correct: The Ottawa ankle rules say an ankle X-ray is needed if there is malleolar-zone pain and any of: bone tenderness along the posterior edge or tip of the distal 6 cm of the lateral malleolus; the same at the medial malleolus; or inability to bear weight for four steps both immediately and in the ED. A foot X-ray is needed for midfoot pain with tenderness at the base of the fifth metatarsal or the navicular, or inability to bear weight. The rules are close to 100% sensitive for clinically significant fractures and reduce unnecessary imaging.

option_explanations.A: Swelling and bruising are common in sprains and are not part of the rules.
option_explanations.B: ATFL soft-tissue tenderness indicates a sprain; it is not an X-ray criterion.
option_explanations.C: Taking four steps, even with a limp, does not meet the weight-bearing criterion.
option_explanations.D: Age is not a criterion in the Ottawa ankle rules.

key_learning_point: Ottawa ankle rules: X-ray if bone tenderness at the posterior edge or tip of the distal 6 cm of either malleolus, or inability to take 4 steps at injury and in the ED.

subtopic: Penetrating chest wound with hypotension, raised JVP and quiet heart sounds: cardiac tamponade
stem:
A 24-year-old man arrives by ambulance at a major trauma centre in Brisbane 25 minutes after being stabbed once in the left chest. He is anxious and pale.

His airway is patent and he is talking. Respiratory rate is 26/min and SpO2 97% on 15 L/min via non-rebreather. Breath sounds are equal, the trachea is central and percussion is resonant bilaterally. Pulse is 128/min and blood pressure 82/60 mmHg, falling by 15 mmHg systolic on inspiration. His neck veins are distended and heart sounds are quiet. There is a 2 cm wound just left of the sternum in the 4th intercostal space, and no other injury.

Two large-bore cannulas are in place and an eFAST is being performed.
lead_in: Which one of the following is the most likely cause of his shock?

options.D: Hypovolaemic shock from an intercostal artery injury
options.E: Blunt cardiac injury with cardiogenic shock

explanation_correct: A stab wound in the 'cardiac box' with shock, distended neck veins and quiet heart sounds (Beck's triad) plus pulsus paradoxus (inspiratory systolic fall above 10 mmHg) indicates obstructive shock from cardiac tamponade. Equal breath sounds, a central trachea and resonant percussion make tension pneumothorax and massive haemothorax unlikely. eFAST will show pericardial fluid. Management is immediate surgical decompression (thoracotomy or sternotomy by the trauma team); pericardiocentesis is only a temporising measure when surgery is unavailable.

option_explanations.A: Also causes shock and distended neck veins, but with absent breath sounds and hyper-resonance on the affected side.
option_explanations.B: Causes hypovolaemic shock with flat neck veins, reduced breath sounds and dullness on the injured side.
option_explanations.D: Hypovolaemia gives collapsed neck veins and does not explain pulsus paradoxus or quiet heart sounds.
option_explanations.E: This follows blunt trauma, with arrhythmia and raised troponin; he has a penetrating wound with signs of a pericardial collection.

key_learning_point: Penetrating 'cardiac box' wound + shock + raised JVP + quiet heart sounds + pulsus paradoxus = tamponade. Urgent surgical decompression.

subtopic: Uncomplicated 6 mm distal ureteric stone: analgesia, tamsulosin and follow-up
stem:
A 41-year-old man presents to an emergency department in Townsville, Queensland, with sudden severe colicky right loin-to-groin pain that began 6 hours ago. He has no fever or rigors. His pain is now controlled after an NSAID, and his observations are normal.

Investigations:
- Urinalysis: blood 3+, nitrites and leucocytes negative
- White cell count 8.2 × 10^9/L (4.0–11.0)
- Creatinine 82 µmol/L (60–110)
- Non-contrast CT KUB: a single 6 mm stone in the right distal ureter 2 cm above the vesicoureteric junction, with mild right hydronephrosis; normal left kidney
lead_in: Which one of the following is the most appropriate management?

options.A: Discharge with an NSAID, tamsulosin, and urology follow-up with repeat imaging
options.D: Oral potassium citrate and review in 3 months
options.E: Oral antibiotics for 7 days and discharge without follow-up

explanation_correct: This is an uncomplicated stone: no infection, normal renal function, two kidneys and controlled pain. Stones of 5–7 mm pass with conservative management in about 60% of cases, and the RACGP review advises NSAIDs as the most effective analgesia and routine tamsulosin 400 µg daily in conservatively managed renal colic (off-label, and not PBS-listed for urolithiasis). Tamsulosin's benefit is mainly for distal stones over 5 mm. He should strain his urine, have follow-up imaging at about 4 weeks (unless the stone is retrieved), and see a urologist if the stone has not passed by about 3 weeks or pain is not controlled. He should return immediately for fever or uncontrolled pain. Urgent drainage is for infection, a single kidney, bilateral obstruction, anuria or poor renal reserve.

option_explanations.B: Urgent decompression is for an obstructed infected kidney, AKI, a solitary kidney or uncontrolled pain.
option_explanations.C: Emergency intervention is not needed for an uncomplicated 6 mm distal stone.
option_explanations.D: Citrate helps prevent some recurrences; it does not help an acute stone pass, and 3 months is too long.
option_explanations.E: He has no infection and needs follow-up to confirm stone passage.

key_learning_point: Uncomplicated distal ureteric stone 5–10 mm: NSAID, tamsulosin and follow-up imaging. Drain urgently only if infected, AKI, solitary kidney or uncontrolled pain.

subtopic: Head injury with a lucid interval and a biconvex collection: extradural haematoma
stem:
A 19-year-old man is brought to an emergency department in Orange, NSW, after being struck on the right side of the head by a cricket ball 2 hours ago. He was unconscious for about a minute, then talked normally and walked to the car. Over the last 30 minutes he has become increasingly drowsy and has vomited twice.

His GCS is now 11 (E3 V3 M5). The right pupil is 5 mm and sluggish; the left is 3 mm and brisk. There is a boggy right temporal swelling. Pulse is 58/min and blood pressure 168/92 mmHg.

Non-contrast CT brain shows a right temporoparietal lens-shaped hyperdense collection that does not cross suture lines, with 6 mm midline shift and an overlying skull fracture.
lead_in: Which one of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

options.D: Diffuse axonal injury
options.E: Cerebral contusion

explanation_correct: A temporal blow with skull fracture, brief loss of consciousness, a lucid interval and then rapid decline is the classic picture of an extradural haematoma, usually from middle meningeal artery injury. On CT it is biconvex because blood strips dura from bone, and it is limited by sutures where dura is firmly attached. An ipsilateral dilating pupil (uncal herniation) and Cushing's response (bradycardia, hypertension) mean emergency neurosurgical evacuation; in a rural hospital, immediate discussion with the neurosurgical centre and retrieval, with airway protection and measures to reduce ICP meanwhile.

option_explanations.A: Subdural blood is crescentic, crosses sutures (not the falx), and usually comes from bridging veins in older people or high-energy injury.
option_explanations.B: Subarachnoid blood fills sulci and cisterns, not a lens-shaped collection with mass effect.
option_explanations.D: DAI causes immediate, persistent coma with little on CT, not a lucid interval.
option_explanations.E: A contusion is intraparenchymal haemorrhage, not a collection between skull and dura.

key_learning_point: Lucid interval + temporal fracture + biconvex collection limited by sutures = extradural haematoma. A blown pupil means emergency evacuation.

subtopic: Expanding neck haematoma with stridor after thyroidectomy: open the wound at the bedside
stem:
A 48-year-old woman had a total thyroidectomy for multinodular goitre 5 hours ago at a private hospital in Adelaide. The nurse calls you, the surgical resident, because she has become anxious and breathless and says her neck feels tight.

She has audible inspiratory stridor, respiratory rate 30/min and SpO2 91% on 6 L/min via face mask. Pulse is 116/min and blood pressure 158/92 mmHg. The neck is visibly swollen and tense under the dressing, and the drain contains little blood. She can speak in short phrases.

The anaesthetist and surgeon have been called and are 10 minutes away.
lead_in: Which one of the following is the most appropriate immediate action?

options.A: Give nebulised adrenaline and IV dexamethasone and observe closely
options.C: Attempt rapid sequence intubation on the ward
options.D: Arrange an urgent neck ultrasound
options.E: Remove the dressing, cut the skin sutures and open the wound, including the strap muscle layer, at the bedside

explanation_correct: Increasing neck swelling with stridor and hypoxia after thyroidectomy is a compressive haematoma, which can obstruct the airway within minutes through venous and lymphatic congestion and laryngeal oedema. A blocked or poorly draining drain does not exclude it. The emergency treatment is immediate bedside wound opening (the 'SCOOP' approach: Skin exposure, Cut sutures, Open skin, Open muscles, Pack) to release the clot, with high-flow oxygen and help called. She then returns to theatre for haemostasis, with the airway managed by an experienced anaesthetist. Decompression comes before attempts at intubation, which are very difficult through a distorted, oedematous airway.

option_explanations.A: These may reduce laryngeal oedema but do not relieve compression by the haematoma.
option_explanations.B: A front-of-neck airway is a last resort; opening the wound is the first step and may relieve the obstruction.
option_explanations.C: Intubation is likely to be very difficult and should not be attempted on the ward before decompression.
option_explanations.D: Imaging delays treatment of a clinical emergency.

key_learning_point: Post-thyroidectomy haematoma with airway compromise: open the wound at the bedside (SCOOP) immediately, then return to theatre.

subtopic: GBS-positive woman in labour with a non-severe delayed penicillin reaction: intrapartum cefazolin
stem:
A 30-year-old woman, gravida 2 para 1, at 39 weeks' gestation presents in spontaneous labour to a maternity unit in Wagga Wagga, NSW. Her rectovaginal swab at 36 weeks grew group B streptococcus. Her membranes are intact, she is afebrile and her cervix is 5 cm dilated.

As a child she developed a mild, itchy, non-blistering rash on day 5 of a course of amoxicillin, which resolved by itself. She has never had hives, swelling, breathing difficulty or a severe skin reaction with any medicine.
lead_in: Which one of the following is the most appropriate intrapartum management?

options.D: No antibiotics, because her membranes are intact
options.E: Oral amoxicillin when she reaches full dilatation

explanation_correct: She is GBS-colonised, so intrapartum antibiotic prophylaxis is recommended to reduce early-onset neonatal GBS disease, ideally starting at least 4 hours before birth. The usual drug is IV benzylpenicillin. For a non-severe, delayed (non-immediate) penicillin reaction, eTG and state maternity guidelines recommend IV cefazolin. Clindamycin is reserved for immediate or severe hypersensitivity and depends on susceptibility, as clindamycin resistance in GBS is increasing.

option_explanations.A: First-line without allergy; with a documented non-severe delayed reaction, cefazolin is used.
option_explanations.C: Reserved for immediate or severe penicillin hypersensitivity, and only if the isolate is susceptible.
option_explanations.D: GBS colonisation is an indication for prophylaxis regardless of membrane status.
option_explanations.E: Oral therapy does not reach adequate levels quickly, amoxicillin is a penicillin, and starting late gives too little time.

key_learning_point: GBS-positive in labour: IV benzylpenicillin; non-severe delayed penicillin reaction: IV cefazolin; immediate or severe reaction: clindamycin if susceptible.

subtopic: Shoulder dystocia: McRoberts manoeuvre first
stem:
A 33-year-old primigravida with insulin-treated gestational diabetes is in the second stage of labour at 40 weeks in a regional hospital in Lismore, NSW. After the head is delivered it retracts against the perineum (the 'turtle sign') and does not restitute. Gentle axial traction fails to deliver the anterior shoulder.

The emergency bell has been pressed, the time of head delivery noted, and the obstetric registrar, a second midwife and the paediatric team are in the room. She is lying flat on the bed.
lead_in: Which one of the following is the most appropriate next step?

options.B: Apply strong downward traction to the head
options.C: Replace the head and perform a caesarean section (Zavanelli manoeuvre)
options.D: Perform an episiotomy as the first step
options.E: Hyperflex and abduct her hips onto her abdomen (McRoberts manoeuvre)

explanation_correct: This is shoulder dystocia. After calling for help, the first manoeuvre is McRoberts: with the woman flat, her hips are hyperflexed and abducted onto her abdomen, which flattens the sacral promontory and rotates the symphysis upwards; it resolves a large proportion of cases. It is usually combined with suprapubic pressure from the side of the fetal back. If these fail, internal manoeuvres (posterior arm delivery, rotational manoeuvres) or the all-fours position follow. Fundal pressure and strong lateral traction must be avoided.

option_explanations.A: Fundal pressure further impacts the shoulder and increases the risk of uterine rupture and brachial plexus injury.
option_explanations.B: Excessive traction greatly increases brachial plexus injury; only gentle axial traction is used.
option_explanations.C: This is a last resort after all other manoeuvres fail.
option_explanations.D: Shoulder dystocia is a bony problem; episiotomy may help access for internal manoeuvres but does not release the shoulder.

key_learning_point: Shoulder dystocia: call for help, then McRoberts plus suprapubic pressure. Avoid fundal pressure and excessive traction.

subtopic: Itch of palms and soles in the third trimester: serum bile acids for intrahepatic cholestasis
stem:
A 32-year-old woman, gravida 1 para 0, at 33 weeks' gestation sees her general practitioner in Shepparton, Victoria, with 10 days of intense itch, worst on her palms and soles and at night. She has no rash apart from scratch marks, and no abdominal pain, headache or visual disturbance. She takes only a pregnancy multivitamin.

Her blood pressure is 118/72 mmHg, urinalysis shows no protein and fetal movements are normal. The skin shows excoriations only.
lead_in: Which one of the following is the most appropriate initial investigation?

options.D: Serum bile acids and liver function tests
options.E: Hepatitis A IgM

explanation_correct: Itch without a primary rash, worst on the palms and soles and at night, in the third trimester suggests intrahepatic cholestasis of pregnancy. Diagnosis rests on raised serum (total) bile acids, often with raised transaminases. The bile acid level helps estimate stillbirth risk (highest at 100 µmol/L or more) and guides timing of birth. If tests are normal but the itch persists, repeat them every 1–2 weeks, as itch can precede biochemical change. Pre-eclampsia and HELLP should be considered, but her BP and urine are normal.

option_explanations.A: This is for pemphigoid gestationis, which causes a blistering rash often starting periumbilically.
option_explanations.B: Allergy testing does not help pregnancy itch without a rash.
option_explanations.C: Gallstones do not cause this pattern of itch without pain.
option_explanations.E: Acute viral hepatitis usually causes malaise, nausea and jaundice; bile acids are the key test here.

key_learning_point: Third-trimester itch of palms and soles without a rash: serum bile acids and LFTs for intrahepatic cholestasis of pregnancy; repeat if normal and itch persists.

subtopic: Early pregnancy bleeding, very high hCG and a 'snowstorm' uterus: complete hydatidiform mole
stem:
A 24-year-old woman, gravida 1, attends an early pregnancy service in Cairns, Queensland, at 10 weeks by dates with 2 weeks of intermittent vaginal bleeding and severe nausea and vomiting. She has lost 3 kg.

Her blood pressure is 142/90 mmHg and pulse 104/min. The uterus is palpable just below the umbilicus. Urinalysis shows ketones 2+ and protein 1+.

Investigations:
- Serum β-hCG 410 000 IU/L
- TSH 0.02 mIU/L (0.4–4.0); free T4 26 pmol/L (9–19)
- Transvaginal ultrasound: enlarged uterus filled with heterogeneous echogenic tissue containing many small cystic spaces; no fetus or gestational sac. Both ovaries contain large multiloculated cysts.
lead_in: Which one of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

options.D: Graves disease with a missed miscarriage
options.E: Complete hydatidiform mole

explanation_correct: Bleeding, a uterus large for dates, hyperemesis, hypertension with proteinuria before 20 weeks, a very high β-hCG, biochemical hyperthyroidism (hCG stimulates the TSH receptor), bilateral theca lutein cysts and a 'snowstorm' appearance with no fetus are classic features of a complete hydatidiform mole, which is diploid and entirely paternal in origin. Treatment is suction curettage with histology, then serial hCG until normal (with reliable contraception) and registration with a trophoblastic disease service, as about 15–20% develop gestational trophoblastic neoplasia.

option_explanations.A: Partial moles are triploid, usually have fetal parts or a sac, and have lower hCG and fewer systemic features.
option_explanations.B: Twins can raise hCG and cause hyperemesis, but ultrasound would show two sacs or fetuses.
option_explanations.C: Retained products do not cause a very high hCG, early pre-eclampsia, thyrotoxicosis or theca lutein cysts.
option_explanations.D: The thyroid changes are explained by hCG, and the ultrasound does not fit a missed miscarriage.

key_learning_point: Very high hCG + uterus large for dates + hyperemesis + early pre-eclampsia ± hyperthyroidism + 'snowstorm' with no fetus = complete mole. Suction curettage and serial hCG.

subtopic: Vulvovaginal candidiasis in pregnancy: topical azole for 7 days, not oral fluconazole
stem:
A 28-year-old woman at 18 weeks' gestation sees her general practitioner in Hervey Bay, Queensland, with 4 days of vulval itch, soreness and a thick white non-malodorous discharge. She has no abdominal pain or fever and no new sexual partner. She has no allergies.

The vulva is red and swollen, with a thick, curd-like white discharge on the vaginal walls. Vaginal pH is 4.2. High vaginal swab microscopy shows budding yeasts and pseudohyphae.
lead_in: Which one of the following is the most appropriate treatment?

options.B: Clotrimazole 500 mg vaginal tablet single dose
options.C: Oral metronidazole 400 mg twice daily for 7 days
options.D: Clotrimazole 100 mg vaginal tablet at night for 7 nights
options.E: No treatment until after the birth

explanation_correct: She has symptomatic vulvovaginal candidiasis confirmed on microscopy with a normal vaginal pH. In pregnancy, eTG recommends an intravaginal azole (clotrimazole or miconazole) for a longer 7-day course, because short courses are less effective in pregnancy. Oral fluconazole should be avoided in pregnancy because of concerns about miscarriage and congenital anomalies. Asymptomatic colonisation does not need treatment, and partners are not routinely treated.

option_explanations.A: First-line outside pregnancy but avoided in pregnancy because of miscarriage and anomaly concerns.
option_explanations.B: Effective outside pregnancy, but 7-day courses are preferred in pregnancy.
option_explanations.C: Metronidazole treats bacterial vaginosis or trichomoniasis, which raise vaginal pH.
option_explanations.E: Symptomatic candidiasis should be treated; topical treatment is low risk.

key_learning_point: Vulvovaginal candidiasis in pregnancy: intravaginal azole for 7 days. Avoid oral fluconazole.

subtopic: Decreased fetal movements at 34 weeks: same-day assessment with CTG
stem:
A 29-year-old woman, gravida 2 para 1, at 34 weeks' gestation phones the birth suite of a hospital in Toowoomba, Queensland, because her baby has been moving much less than usual since yesterday. She is asked to come in and arrives 40 minutes later. Her pregnancy has been uncomplicated, with a normal 20-week ultrasound.

Her blood pressure is 116/74 mmHg, and she has no pain, bleeding or fluid loss. Symphysis–fundal height is 33 cm. The fetal heart is heard on handheld Doppler at 140/min.
lead_in: Which one of the following is the most appropriate next step?

options.B: Reassure her because a fetal heartbeat has been heard
options.C: Ask her to count kicks at home for 2 hours and call back
options.D: Induce labour today
options.E: Arrange an outpatient growth ultrasound in 2 weeks

explanation_correct: Decreased fetal movements can signal fetal compromise and are associated with stillbirth. The Australian Stillbirth CRE guideline (part of the Safer Baby Bundle) recommends that, after confirming the fetal heart, a woman at 28 weeks or more has a CTG (computerised where available), together with assessment of risk factors for growth restriction and stillbirth. Ultrasound for growth, liquor and umbilical artery Doppler is arranged (ideally within 24 hours) when there are risk factors, growth concerns, an abnormal CTG or recurrent decreased movements. Women should never be told to count kicks at home instead of attending.

option_explanations.B: Hearing the fetal heart does not exclude compromise; a CTG is needed.
option_explanations.C: Formal kick counting is not recommended; she needs prompt assessment in person.
option_explanations.D: Birth may be needed if assessment shows compromise, but immediate induction at 34 weeks is not the first step.
option_explanations.E: Waiting 2 weeks is inappropriate; if needed, ultrasound should be within 24 hours.

key_learning_point: Decreased fetal movements at 28 weeks or more: same-day assessment, confirm the fetal heart, then CTG; add ultrasound if there are risk factors or concerns.

subtopic: Episodic inconsolable crying with pallor and lethargy in an infant: ultrasound for intussusception
stem:
A 9-month-old boy is brought to an emergency department in Ballarat, Victoria. Since this morning he has had episodes every 15–20 minutes of screaming, drawing up his legs and going pale, each lasting a few minutes. Between episodes he is unusually sleepy. He has vomited three times. He had a cold last week and passed a normal stool this morning.

His temperature is 37.4 °C, pulse 150/min and capillary refill 2 seconds. Between episodes his abdomen is soft, with a vague sausage-shaped mass in the right upper quadrant. There is no blood in the nappy.
lead_in: Which one of the following is the most appropriate initial investigation?

options.D: Stool culture and viral PCR
options.E: Abdominal ultrasound

explanation_correct: Episodic colicky pain with pallor and drawing up of the legs, lethargy between episodes, vomiting and a right upper quadrant mass in an infant aged 6–18 months suggests ileocolic intussusception, often with lymphoid hyperplasia after a viral illness as the lead point. Redcurrant jelly stool is a late sign; its absence does not exclude the diagnosis. Ultrasound is the investigation of choice ('target' or 'doughnut' sign): highly sensitive and radiation-free. If confirmed without peritonitis or perforation, treatment is air (pneumatic) enema reduction by an experienced paediatric radiology team with surgical backup, plus IV access and fluids.

option_explanations.A: An X-ray may show obstruction or free gas but is neither sensitive nor specific for intussusception.
option_explanations.B: CT is unnecessary and involves radiation; ultrasound is accurate in children.
option_explanations.C: This is for suspected malrotation with volvulus (bilious vomiting in a neonate).
option_explanations.D: Gastroenteritis does not explain episodic pain, pallor, lethargy and a mass, and waiting delays diagnosis.

key_learning_point: Infant with episodic screaming, pallor and lethargy ± a mass: ultrasound for intussusception. No redcurrant jelly stool does not exclude it.

subtopic: Pyloric stenosis with hypochloraemic alkalosis: correct fluids and electrolytes before pyloromyotomy
stem:
A 5-week-old boy is transferred to a paediatric surgical unit in Melbourne with 5 days of forceful non-bilious vomiting after every feed; he seems hungry straight afterwards. He was born at term weighing 3.6 kg and now weighs 3.7 kg.

He has a sunken fontanelle and dry mucous membranes; capillary refill is 2 seconds. An olive-shaped epigastric mass is felt during a test feed. Ultrasound shows pyloric muscle thickness 5 mm and channel length 19 mm.

Capillary blood gas:
- pH 7.53
- Bicarbonate 36 mmol/L (22–28)
- Chloride 86 mmol/L (95–110)
- Potassium 2.9 mmol/L (3.5–5.5)
- Sodium 132 mmol/L (135–145)
- Glucose 4.2 mmol/L
lead_in: Which one of the following is the most appropriate management?

options.A: IV 0.9% sodium chloride with 5% glucose and added potassium, then pyloromyotomy once chloride and bicarbonate have normalised
options.C: IV 5% glucose alone at maintenance rate
options.D: IV sodium bicarbonate to correct the low sodium
options.E: Thickened feeds and a proton pump inhibitor

explanation_correct: He has infantile hypertrophic pyloric stenosis, confirmed on ultrasound, with the typical hypochloraemic, hypokalaemic metabolic alkalosis caused by loss of gastric acid. RCH says correcting dehydration, electrolyte and acid–base abnormalities is the priority, and surgery is delayed until they are corrected. It is particularly important to wait for the serum bicarbonate to normalise, because a metabolic alkalosis risks postoperative hypoventilation and apnoea. Fluids: 0.9% sodium chloride boluses only if needed for resuscitation, then 0.9% sodium chloride + 5% glucose for deficit and maintenance, with potassium added once urine output is adequate (1–2 mL/kg/h). Stop oral feeds, and pass a nasogastric tube if vomiting continues. Pyloromyotomy follows once the biochemistry has normalised.

option_explanations.B: Operating while alkalotic and hypokalaemic increases anaesthetic risk, particularly postoperative apnoea.
option_explanations.C: RCH uses 0.9% sodium chloride + 5% glucose; glucose alone gives no sodium or chloride to correct the hypochloraemic alkalosis and risks hyponatraemia.
option_explanations.D: Bicarbonate would worsen the metabolic alkalosis; the deficit is corrected with 0.9% saline.
option_explanations.E: This treats reflux; pyloric stenosis is a mechanical obstruction needing surgery after resuscitation.

key_learning_point: Pyloric stenosis: correct the hypochloraemic hypokalaemic alkalosis with 0.9% saline + 5% glucose + KCl before pyloromyotomy, to avoid postoperative apnoea.

subtopic: Fever without a source in a non-toilet-trained infant: urine collection method for culture
stem:
A 7-month-old girl is referred by her general practitioner in Bathurst, NSW, to the local emergency department with 2 days of fever up to 39.4 °C, poor feeding and irritability. She has no cough, coryza, rash, diarrhoea or vomiting and is fully immunised.

Her temperature is 39.1 °C, pulse 158/min and capillary refill 2 seconds. She is irritable but consolable and well perfused. Ears, throat and chest are normal, with no rash or neck stiffness. She is assessed as not toxic. A urinary tract infection is suspected. She is not toilet-trained.
lead_in: Which one of the following is the most appropriate way to collect urine for culture?

options.A: Urine bag applied to the perineum
options.B: Urine squeezed from a wet disposable nappy
options.C: Clean-catch urine or a catheter specimen
options.D: Cotton-wool ball placed in the nappy
options.E: No sample; start empirical oral antibiotics

explanation_correct: UTI is a common cause of fever without a focus in infants, and a urine sample suitable for culture is needed before antibiotics. For a child who is not toilet-trained, Australian paediatric guidelines (such as RCH) recommend a clean-catch specimen, which can be encouraged by suprapubic stimulation (the Quick-Wee method), or a catheter specimen; suprapubic aspiration is an alternative mainly in young infants. Bag specimens are frequently contaminated and should not be sent for culture; a negative bag dipstick may help exclude UTI in a well child, but a positive result must be confirmed on a proper sample.

option_explanations.A: Bag specimens have high contamination rates and many false positives; not suitable for culture.
option_explanations.B: Nappy urine is heavily contaminated and unsuitable for culture.
option_explanations.D: Pad samples have high contamination rates and are not recommended for diagnosis.
option_explanations.E: Without culture, a UTI cannot be confirmed, treatment cannot be guided by sensitivities, and follow-up imaging decisions are compromised.

key_learning_point: Urine culture in a child who is not toilet-trained: clean catch (Quick-Wee) or catheter (or SPA). Never culture a bag specimen.

subtopic: Knee pain and limp in an overweight adolescent with obligatory external rotation: slipped capital femoral epiphysis
stem:
A 13-year-old boy is brought to his general practitioner in Gladstone, Queensland, with 4 weeks of aching left knee pain and a limp, without injury or fever. He is otherwise well. His BMI is above the 97th centile.

He walks with an antalgic, out-toeing gait on the left. The left knee is normal, with full range of movement and no effusion or tenderness. When the left hip is flexed it rolls into external rotation, and internal rotation is markedly reduced and painful. The right hip is normal.
lead_in: Which one of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

options.D: Slipped capital femoral epiphysis
options.E: Patellofemoral pain syndrome

explanation_correct: An overweight early adolescent with a limp, knee pain (referred from the hip via the obturator nerve), a normal knee, loss of hip internal rotation and obligatory external rotation on hip flexion has SCFE until proven otherwise. He needs urgent AP and frog-leg lateral X-rays of both hips (the lateral view shows mild slips missed on AP, and the other side is often involved), non-weight-bearing and urgent orthopaedic referral for in situ fixation. Delay increases the risk of slip progression and avascular necrosis.

option_explanations.A: Causes pain and tenderness over the tibial tuberosity; his knee is normal and his hip is abnormal.
option_explanations.B: Perthes usually affects boys aged 4–8, not overweight adolescents.
option_explanations.C: Occurs at ages 3–8 after a viral illness and settles within about 2 weeks.
option_explanations.E: Causes anterior knee pain on stairs or squatting with a normal hip examination.

key_learning_point: Knee pain + limp in an overweight adolescent with loss of hip internal rotation = SCFE until proven otherwise. AP and frog-leg lateral X-rays of both hips; non-weight-bearing; urgent orthopaedics.

subtopic: Pale toddler drinking large volumes of cow's milk: iron deficiency anaemia
stem:
A 2-year-old girl is brought to a community health clinic in Logan, Queensland, because her mother thinks she looks pale. She is a fussy eater who eats little meat and drinks about 1.2 litres of cow's milk a day, mostly from a bottle. She is active and developing normally. There is no family history of anaemia.

She is pale, with normal growth, and has no jaundice, bruising, lymphadenopathy or hepatosplenomegaly.

Investigations:
- Haemoglobin 88 g/L (105–135)
- MCV 61 fL (70–86)
- Reticulocytes low
- White cells and platelets normal
- Blood film: microcytic hypochromic red cells with pencil cells
lead_in: Which one of the following is the most likely cause of her anaemia?

options.A: Iron deficiency from excessive cow's milk intake
options.D: Anaemia of chronic disease
options.E: Transient erythroblastopenia of childhood

explanation_correct: Excessive cow's milk is the commonest cause of iron deficiency anaemia in toddlers: it is low in iron, displaces iron-rich foods and can cause occult intestinal blood loss in young children. A microcytic hypochromic anaemia with pencil cells, low reticulocytes and normal white cells and platelets fits; a low ferritin confirms it. Management is oral iron, continued for about 3 months after haemoglobin normalises, limiting cow's milk to about 500 mL a day, weaning from the bottle and increasing iron-rich foods. A haemoglobin rise within about 4 weeks confirms the diagnosis.

option_explanations.B: Causes microcytosis with mild or no anaemia, a normal or high red cell count and target cells.
option_explanations.C: Can cause microcytic anaemia with basophilic stippling, but there is no exposure history or pica.
option_explanations.D: She has no chronic illness, and it is usually normocytic or only mildly microcytic.
option_explanations.E: TEC causes a normocytic anaemia, not marked microcytosis.

key_learning_point: Toddler drinking well over 500 mL of cow's milk a day with microcytic anaemia: iron deficiency. Oral iron and limit milk to about 500 mL a day.
