subtopic: IgA vasculitis (Henoch–Schönlein purpura): urinalysis and blood pressure monitoring for nephritis
stem:
A 6-year-old boy is reviewed by his general practitioner in Coffs Harbour, NSW, 4 days after IgA vasculitis (Henoch–Schönlein purpura) was diagnosed in the emergency department. He has palpable purpura on his buttocks and legs, sore ankles and occasional colicky abdominal pain, controlled with paracetamol. He had a sore throat 2 weeks ago and is eating and drinking.

His blood pressure is 98/60 mmHg (normal for age). His ankles are mildly swollen and his abdomen is soft and non-tender.

In the ED his full blood count, coagulation and creatinine were normal and urinalysis was negative. His mother asks what follow-up he needs.
lead_in: Which one of the following is the most appropriate follow-up to detect the most important long-term complication?

options.A: Weekly full blood count for 1 month
options.B: Repeat urinalysis only if he develops swelling
options.D: Blood pressure and urinalysis weekly for the first month, fortnightly to week 12, then at 6 and 12 months
options.E: Oral prednisolone to prevent kidney disease

explanation_correct: Most childhood IgA vasculitis (HSP) resolves within about 4 weeks, but renal involvement is the main long-term risk and is usually asymptomatic. According to RCH, 90% of children who develop renal complications do so within 2 months of onset and 97% within 6 months, so a normal first urinalysis does not exclude later nephritis. If the first urinalysis is normal (or shows only microscopic haematuria), RCH recommends a clinical review with BP and urinalysis weekly for the first month, fortnightly from weeks 5–12, and single reviews at 6 and 12 months, going back to weekly checks if the disease flares. If urinalysis is normal at 12 months, no further follow-up is needed. Hypertension, proteinuria or macroscopic haematuria at any stage needs paediatric review, and persistent proteinuria needs renal referral. Steroids do not change the rate of long-term renal complications.

option_explanations.A: Platelets are normal in IgA vasculitis, and repeated blood counts do not detect nephritis.
option_explanations.B: Nephritis is often silent and can follow a normal first urinalysis; scheduled testing is needed.
option_explanations.C: Ultrasound does not detect glomerulonephritis.
option_explanations.E: Steroids may help severe abdominal pain but do not prevent nephritis.

key_learning_point: IgA vasculitis (HSP): BP + urinalysis weekly for month 1, fortnightly to week 12, then at 6 and 12 months (RCH). Renal involvement is usually silent; steroids do not prevent it.

subtopic: Before starting lithium: baseline renal, thyroid and calcium tests
stem:
A 33-year-old woman with bipolar I disorder sees her psychiatrist in Adelaide 3 months after a manic episode that needed admission. She has recovered on quetiapine but has gained 9 kg and wants to change. They agree to start lithium carbonate for maintenance. She uses a copper IUD and takes no other medicines.

Her blood pressure is 118/76 mmHg and BMI 29 kg/m². There is no goitre.
lead_in: Which one of the following sets of baseline tests is most important before starting lithium?

options.A: Full blood count, liver function tests and an EEG
options.C: Electrolytes, creatinine with eGFR, TSH and serum calcium
options.D: A baseline serum lithium level
options.E: Urine drug screen and HLA-B*15:02 testing

explanation_correct: Lithium is cleared almost entirely by the kidneys and has a narrow therapeutic range. Long-term use can cause chronic kidney disease and nephrogenic diabetes insipidus, hypothyroidism, and hyperparathyroidism with hypercalcaemia. Before starting, check electrolytes, creatinine/eGFR, thyroid function and calcium, plus weight, a pregnancy test where relevant, and an ECG if there is cardiac risk or older age. On treatment, 12-hour post-dose levels are monitored, and renal, thyroid and calcium tests are repeated regularly (typically 6-monthly).

option_explanations.A: LFTs matter more for valproate and carbamazepine, and an EEG is not needed; these miss lithium's key target organs.
option_explanations.B: These are antipsychotic metabolic monitoring tests, not the key lithium baseline.
option_explanations.D: There is no point measuring lithium before starting; levels are checked after about 5 days on a stable dose.
option_explanations.E: HLA-B*15:02 testing is before carbamazepine in some Asian ancestries; it is irrelevant to lithium.

key_learning_point: Before lithium: electrolytes, creatinine/eGFR, TSH and calcium (plus weight, pregnancy test, ± ECG). Then 12-hour levels and 6-monthly renal, thyroid and calcium.

subtopic: OCD with a partial response to low-dose SSRI: increase the dose and continue exposure and response prevention
stem:
A 26-year-old accountant sees her general practitioner in Darwin for review of obsessive-compulsive disorder. She has intrusive fears of contamination and spent about 3 hours a day handwashing and cleaning. Six weeks ago she started sertraline 50 mg daily and has had four sessions of exposure and response prevention (ERP) with a psychologist under a Mental Health Treatment Plan. She now spends about 2 hours a day on rituals and has mild nausea only. She has no suicidal thoughts and no alcohol or drug use.

Her Y-BOCS score has fallen from 28 to 24.
lead_in: Which one of the following is the most appropriate next step?

options.B: Increase sertraline gradually towards a higher dose (such as 150–200 mg daily) and continue ERP
options.D: Stop ERP and continue sertraline 50 mg alone
options.E: Add diazepam 5 mg as needed for distress

explanation_correct: She has had a partial response after only 6 weeks on a low SSRI dose. Australian Prescriber (Therapeutic Guidelines) notes that OCD responds to SSRIs more slowly than depression and that most patients need doses in the higher therapeutic range (sertraline 50–200 mg/day in studies). The dose can go up every 2 weeks as tolerated, and an SSRI should be trialled at its maximum dose for at least 12 weeks before it is judged ineffective. Gains usually plateau at about 12 weeks. ERP has the strongest psychological evidence, and combining it with an SSRI works better than either alone, so ERP should continue. Clomipramine is usually kept for after two failed SSRI trials, OCD tends not to respond to benzodiazepines, and treatment-resistant patients should be referred to a psychiatrist.

option_explanations.A: Clomipramine is usually reserved until two SSRI trials have failed, because it is less well tolerated.
option_explanations.C: Antipsychotic augmentation is for SSRI-resistant OCD after an adequate trial; premature here.
option_explanations.D: ERP is the most effective psychological treatment and should continue.
option_explanations.E: Benzodiazepines do not treat OCD, can undermine exposure work and risk dependence.

key_learning_point: OCD: SSRIs often need higher doses and 8–12 weeks. Optimise the dose and continue ERP before switching or augmenting.

subtopic: Cognitive impairment in an older person: features favouring depression over dementia
stem:
A 74-year-old retired teacher is brought to her general practitioner in Wollongong, NSW, by her daughter, who is worried about her memory. Over 3 months since her husband's death she has stopped going to her book club, forgets appointments and cannot concentrate on the newspaper. She wakes at 4 am and has lost 5 kg. She complains that her memory is 'useless'.

On cognitive testing she often answers 'I don't know' and gives up quickly, but with encouragement gets several answers right. Her performance varies from item to item without a clear pattern. She is oriented to time and place, well groomed and has no focal neurological signs. FBC, electrolytes, calcium, TSH, B12 and folate are normal.
lead_in: Which one of the following is the most likely explanation for her cognitive symptoms?

options.A: Major depressive disorder with cognitive impairment
options.D: Normal grief
options.E: Frontotemporal dementia

explanation_correct: Subacute onset over weeks to months after a clear trigger (bereavement), depressive features (withdrawal, early morning waking, weight loss), prominent self-reported memory complaints, 'I don't know' answers, poor effort and inconsistent performance that improves with encouragement all favour depression causing cognitive impairment (formerly 'pseudodementia'). In early Alzheimer disease onset is insidious, patients tend to minimise or lack awareness of deficits, try hard but give wrong answers or confabulate, and short-term memory loss is consistent. Treating the depression often improves cognition, but she needs follow-up because late-life depression can precede dementia.

option_explanations.B: Onset is insidious, patients often minimise problems and try hard but answer wrongly.
option_explanations.C: Delirium is an acute, fluctuating disturbance of attention over hours to days; she is oriented with a 3-month history.
option_explanations.D: Grief does not usually cause this degree of withdrawal, weight loss, early waking and cognitive impairment over 3 months.
option_explanations.E: Causes early personality, behaviour or language change, usually before 65.

key_learning_point: Depression vs dementia: subacute onset, memory complaints, 'don't know' answers and variable effort suggest depression; insidious onset, minimised deficits and wrong answers despite effort suggest dementia.

subtopic: Starting olanzapine in first-episode psychosis: baseline cardiometabolic monitoring
stem:
A 21-year-old man is seen by an early psychosis service in Geelong, Victoria, for a first episode of psychosis. He agrees to start olanzapine. He has no medical history. His father has type 2 diabetes. He smokes 15 cigarettes a day and does not use other drugs.

The registrar is planning his physical health monitoring.
lead_in: Which one of the following is the most appropriate set of baseline measurements before olanzapine is started?

options.B: Weight, waist circumference, blood pressure, fasting glucose or HbA1c, and fasting lipids
options.D: A 12-lead ECG only
options.E: Troponin and CRP weekly for 4 weeks

explanation_correct: Second-generation antipsychotics, especially olanzapine and clozapine, cause weight gain and increase the risk of diabetes and dyslipidaemia, particularly in young people with a first episode. RANZCP guidance and the Australian 'Positive Cardiometabolic Health' algorithm recommend baseline weight/BMI, waist circumference, blood pressure, fasting glucose or HbA1c and fasting lipids, with smoking and family history, then close monitoring (weight at each visit in the first months; bloods at about 3 months then regularly). Early weight gain should prompt lifestyle intervention, a switch to a lower-risk agent or metformin. He should also be offered smoking cessation support.

option_explanations.A: Prolactin matters more for risperidone and amisulpride, and an EEG is not routine.
option_explanations.C: Weekly FBC is for clozapine (neutropenia), not olanzapine.
option_explanations.D: An ECG has a role in some patients but alone misses olanzapine's major metabolic risks.
option_explanations.E: This is monitoring for clozapine-induced myocarditis.

key_learning_point: Before an antipsychotic (especially olanzapine): weight/BMI, waist, BP, fasting glucose or HbA1c, lipids and smoking history; then monitor closely.

subtopic: Insomnia, agitation, delusions about the baby and confusion 8 days postpartum: postpartum psychosis
stem:
A 29-year-old woman gave birth to her first baby by caesarean 8 days ago at a hospital in Hobart, Tasmania. Her partner brings her to the emergency department because for 2 days she has hardly slept, talks rapidly and paces the house at night. She says the baby has been 'swapped' and the nurses are poisoning her milk. At times she seems confused about where she is. Her mother had bipolar disorder.

She is afebrile with normal observations and a healing wound. FBC, electrolytes, calcium, glucose, TSH and urinalysis are normal. There is no drug or alcohol use.
lead_in: Which one of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

options.D: Postpartum thyroiditis
options.E: Delirium due to puerperal sepsis

explanation_correct: Rapid onset of insomnia, pressured speech, agitation, delusions involving the baby and fluctuating confusion within the first 2 weeks after birth, in a first-time mother with a family history of bipolar disorder, is typical of postpartum psychosis, which is often a presentation of bipolar disorder. It is a psychiatric emergency because of the risks of suicide and infanticide. She needs urgent psychiatric assessment and admission, ideally to a mother–baby unit, with the baby's safety ensured. Organic causes (infection, thyroid, electrolytes, drugs) should be excluded, as here.

option_explanations.A: Common in the first week with tearfulness and lability, but no psychosis or confusion; resolves within about 2 weeks.
option_explanations.C: Low mood and anhedonia over weeks to months; rapid psychotic features and confusion suggest psychosis.
option_explanations.D: Usually 1–6 months after birth; her TSH is normal.
option_explanations.E: She is afebrile with normal observations, a healing wound and normal bloods.

key_learning_point: Psychotic and manic symptoms with confusion in the first 2 weeks postpartum (especially with a bipolar family history) = postpartum psychosis: emergency admission, ideally to a mother–baby unit.

subtopic: Chronic insomnia disorder in primary care: CBT for insomnia first line
stem:
A 46-year-old man sees his general practitioner in Bunbury, Western Australia, with 8 months of difficulty getting to sleep and staying asleep on most nights. He lies awake worrying about not sleeping, checks the clock and naps on the couch in the evening. He feels tired and irritable at work. He drinks two coffees in the morning and 2 standard drinks most nights 'to help him sleep'. He does not snore and his partner has seen no breathing pauses. He has no low mood or anxiety apart from about sleep. His examination is normal and BMI 24 kg/m².

He asks for 'something to help me sleep'.
lead_in: Which one of the following is the most appropriate initial management?

options.B: Temazepam 10 mg at night for 3 months
options.C: Zolpidem 10 mg at night long term
options.D: Low-dose quetiapine at night
options.E: Refer for diagnostic polysomnography

explanation_correct: He has chronic insomnia disorder (difficulty initiating or maintaining sleep at least 3 nights a week for 3 months or more with daytime impairment) with typical perpetuating factors: worry about sleep, clock-watching, evening naps and alcohol. CBT-I (stimulus control, sleep restriction, cognitive therapy, sleep hygiene education) is the recommended first-line treatment in Australian guidance (RACGP, Australasian Sleep Association), with durable benefit; it can be delivered by a psychologist, a trained GP or a digital program. He should reduce alcohol, which fragments later sleep. Hypnotics are only for short-term use in selected cases.

option_explanations.B: Benzodiazepines are not recommended for chronic insomnia because of tolerance, dependence, falls and cognitive effects.
option_explanations.C: Z-drugs share benzodiazepine risks and can cause complex sleep behaviours.
option_explanations.D: Quetiapine has metabolic and other harms and is not recommended for insomnia.
option_explanations.E: Nothing suggests sleep apnoea or another primary sleep disorder; insomnia is a clinical diagnosis.

key_learning_point: Chronic insomnia: CBT-I first line. Avoid long-term hypnotics and antipsychotics for sleep.

subtopic: Calculating sensitivity and specificity from a 2 × 2 table
stem:
A new point-of-care troponin test is evaluated in 1000 adults presenting with chest pain to rural emergency departments in Western Australia. The reference standard is a final diagnosis of acute myocardial infarction based on laboratory high-sensitivity troponin and specialist review.

| | MI present | MI absent | Total |
|---|---|---|---|
| Test positive | 90 | 45 | 135 |
| Test negative | 10 | 855 | 865 |
| Total | 100 | 900 | 1000 |
lead_in: Which one of the following correctly gives the sensitivity and specificity of the new test?

options.D: Sensitivity 10%; specificity 5%
options.E: Sensitivity 90%; specificity 95%

explanation_correct: Sensitivity = true positives ÷ all with disease = 90 ÷ 100 = 90%. Specificity = true negatives ÷ all without disease = 855 ÷ 900 = 95%. For comparison, PPV = 90 ÷ 135 = 67% and NPV = 855 ÷ 865 = 98.8%. Sensitivity and specificity are properties of the test and do not change with prevalence; predictive values do.

option_explanations.A: These are the PPV (90/135) and NPV (855/865, about 99%).
option_explanations.B: The values are swapped; sensitivity comes from people with MI (90/100).
option_explanations.C: Specificity is from people without MI (855/900 = 95%), not from test-negatives (855/865).
option_explanations.D: These are the false-negative rate (10/100) and false-positive rate (45/900).

key_learning_point: Sensitivity = TP/(TP+FN); specificity = TN/(TN+FP): calculate down the disease columns. Predictive values run across the test rows.

subtopic: An association that disappears after stratification: confounding
stem:
A cohort study in an Australian regional city follows 10 000 adults for 10 years. Crude analysis shows that people who drink more than 4 cups of coffee a day have a higher risk of lung cancer than lighter drinkers (relative risk 2.4; 95% CI 1.8–3.2).

The analysis is then stratified by smoking status:
- Never-smokers: relative risk 1.02 (95% CI 0.70–1.48)
- Current smokers: relative risk 1.05 (95% CI 0.85–1.30)

Heavy coffee drinkers were much more likely to smoke than light coffee drinkers.
lead_in: Which one of the following best explains these findings?

options.A: Smoking is an effect modifier of the association
options.B: The crude result is due to selection bias
options.C: Smoking is a confounder of the association between coffee and lung cancer
options.D: Smoking is on the causal pathway between coffee and lung cancer
options.E: The stratified results are due to chance and the crude result should be reported

explanation_correct: A confounder is associated with the exposure (smokers drink more coffee), is an independent risk factor for the outcome (smoking causes lung cancer) and is not on the causal pathway. After stratification by smoking the association disappears in both strata (RRs about 1 and similar), so the crude association was produced by smoking: confounding. Effect modification would show different stratum-specific effects. Confounding is controlled by stratification, multivariable adjustment, matching, restriction or randomisation.

option_explanations.A: Effect modification means the association differs between strata; here both strata are similar and null.
option_explanations.B: Selection bias arises from recruitment or retention and would not be removed by stratifying on smoking.
option_explanations.D: Coffee does not cause smoking, so smoking is not a mediator.
option_explanations.E: Consistent strata with reasonably narrow intervals make chance unlikely; the crude result is misleading.

key_learning_point: Association disappears with similar results in each stratum = confounding; different results across strata = effect modification.

subtopic: Funded recombinant zoster vaccine for an Aboriginal adult aged 50 or over: eligibility and schedule
stem:
A 52-year-old Aboriginal man has a health check at an Aboriginal Community Controlled Health Service in Alice Springs, Northern Territory. He has type 2 diabetes and hypertension and is not immunocompromised. He had chickenpox as a child and has never had herpes zoster. His other recommended vaccines are up to date.

He asks about the shingles vaccine because his uncle recently had shingles.
lead_in: Which one of the following is the most appropriate advice?

options.A: He must wait until age 65 for a funded vaccine
options.B: He is eligible for 2 doses of recombinant zoster vaccine (Shingrix) funded under the National Immunisation Program, given 2–6 months apart
options.C: He needs varicella serology before vaccination
options.D: He should have a single funded dose of live zoster vaccine (Zostavax)
options.E: He is eligible for only 1 funded dose of recombinant zoster vaccine

explanation_correct: The Australian Immunisation Handbook (updated 30 Sep 2026) recommends zoster vaccine for all immunocompetent people aged 50 and over, and says Shingrix is NIP-funded for non-Indigenous people aged 65 and over, Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander people aged 50 and over, and people aged 18 and over with moderate or severe immunocompromise. He is a 52-year-old Aboriginal man, so he is eligible for funded vaccine. Immunocompetent people get 2 doses 2–6 months apart; immunocompromised people get 2 doses 1–2 months apart. Shingrix is non-live and is the only zoster vaccine available in Australia. Serology is not recommended before or after vaccination, and a history of chickenpox is not needed.

option_explanations.A: Funded eligibility starts at 50 for Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander people.
option_explanations.C: The Handbook states serological testing is not recommended before or after zoster vaccination.
option_explanations.D: Zostavax has been removed; Shingrix is now the only zoster vaccine available in Australia.
option_explanations.E: Shingrix needs 2 doses, and both are funded for eligible people.

key_learning_point: Funded Shingrix (2 doses, 2–6 months apart): 65+, Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander people 50+, and eligible immunocompromised people 18+.

subtopic: A 15-year-old requesting contraception without parental knowledge: mature minor assessment
stem:
A 15-year-old girl attends a general practice in Penrith, NSW, alone. She asks to start the contraceptive pill because she has been in a sexual relationship with her 16-year-old boyfriend for 3 months. She says the relationship is consensual and she does not feel pressured, and asks the GP not to tell her parents. She can explain what the pill does, its risks and side effects, and that it does not protect against sexually transmitted infections.

There are no concerns about abuse, coercion or exploitation, and she has no contraindications to the combined pill.
lead_in: Which one of the following is the most appropriate management?

options.A: Tell her parental consent is required under 16
options.B: Prescribe if she is assessed as a mature minor, maintain confidentiality, and offer STI testing and condom advice
options.C: Make a mandatory report to child protection because she is under 16
options.D: Refuse to prescribe but provide condoms
options.E: Prescribe and phone her parents to let them know

explanation_correct: Under common law (Gillick competence, endorsed in Australia in Marion's case), a person under 18 can consent to their own treatment if they have sufficient understanding and maturity to understand fully what is proposed, including risks and alternatives. She appears to. The GP should document the competence assessment, prescribe, respect confidentiality, encourage (but not require) involvement of a trusted adult, and offer STI testing, condoms and information about long-acting reversible contraception. Her partner is of similar age and there are no concerns about coercion, so on these facts there is no mandatory report; a HEEADSSS psychosocial assessment should still screen for exploitation.

option_explanations.A: There is no fixed age requirement for parental consent to contraception when the young person is a mature minor.
option_explanations.C: Consensual activity between similar-aged adolescents does not by itself trigger a report; reporting depends on risk of significant harm (abuse, coercion, a large age gap).
option_explanations.D: Refusing effective contraception to a competent young person increases her risk of unintended pregnancy.
option_explanations.E: Disclosure without consent breaches the confidentiality of a competent minor without serious risk of harm.

key_learning_point: Under-16s can consent to contraception if Gillick-competent. Assess and document competence, keep confidentiality, and screen for abuse or coercion.

subtopic: New HIV diagnosis with refusal to inform a regular partner: partner notification and public health escalation
stem:
A 34-year-old man is told by his general practitioner in Brisbane that his HIV test is positive; his viral load is 85 000 copies/mL. He has a female partner of 2 years with whom he has condomless sex. He refuses to tell her because he fears she will leave him, and asks the GP not to say anything. She is not a patient of the practice. He agrees to see an HIV specialist.

The GP has explained the transmission risk to his partner and the benefits of starting antiretroviral therapy soon.
lead_in: Which one of the following is the most appropriate next step for the GP?

options.A: Phone his partner today and tell her the diagnosis
options.B: Respect his wishes completely and take no further action
options.C: Notify the police that he is putting his partner at risk
options.D: Refuse further care until he informs his partner
options.E: Continue counselling and support, offer provider-assisted partner notification, and seek advice from the Queensland HIV Public Health Team if he remains unwilling

explanation_correct: At diagnosis, every person with HIV should get treatment, psychosocial support, counselling about preventing transmission, and help to make sure at-risk partners are identified and tested. Contact tracing can be patient-led or provider-assisted (ASHM). Rapid ART aiming for an undetectable viral load (U=U), with condoms or PrEP for the partner meanwhile, greatly reduces the risk. The Queensland Health guideline, which follows the 2018 National Guidelines for Managing HIV Transmission Risk Behaviours, uses a stepped, least-restrictive framework under the Public Health Act 2005. At Level 1 the treating clinician provides case management (counselling, education and support). If the person is unwilling or unable to change risk behaviours, the clinician should seek help from the HIV Public Health Team and/or notify the chair of the HIV advisory panel. Only then can escalation follow (Level 2 department-supported management, then behavioural or detention orders). The GP should not disclose independently as a first step, and must handle any identifying information within confidentiality law.

option_explanations.A: Unilateral disclosure as a first step breaches confidentiality; counselling and the formal public health pathway come first.
option_explanations.B: Confidentiality is not absolute when a third party is at serious risk; the GP must keep working on notification and escalate if needed.
option_explanations.C: Police are not the appropriate first contact; public health law and the health department manage this.
option_explanations.D: Ending care harms him and increases transmission risk.

key_learning_point: HIV partner notification: counsel, offer provider-assisted or anonymous notification, start ART (U=U), and escalate to the public health unit if refusal continues. Do not disclose unilaterally first.

subtopic: Gynaecological history from a patient with limited English: professional interpreter, not a family member
stem: A 58-year-old woman who arrived from Afghanistan 6 months ago on a humanitarian visa attends a general practice in Dandenong, Victoria. She speaks Dari and very little English. Her 14-year-old son, who speaks fluent English, has come with her and offers to interpret. She has come about 'women's problems', and the GP needs to take a full gynaecological history and discuss a possible pelvic examination.
lead_in: Which one of the following is the most appropriate way to take her history?

options.A: Ask her son to interpret because he is fluent
options.B: Use a translation app on the GP's phone
options.C: Use a professional Dari interpreter, by phone through TIS National if one is not available in person
options.D: Take the history in simple English with gestures
options.E: Ask her to return with an adult relative to interpret

explanation_correct: Professional interpreters should be used when a patient has limited English, especially for sensitive histories and consent to examination. Family members, and particularly children, should not interpret: they may filter or change information, the topic may be embarrassing, it can harm the child, and confidentiality is lost. TIS National provides free phone and on-site interpreting for medical practitioners for Medicare-rebatable services. The GP should also ask whether she would prefer a female interpreter (and a female doctor).

option_explanations.A: Using a child for a gynaecological history risks inaccuracy and embarrassment, harms the child and breaches confidentiality.
option_explanations.B: Machine translation is not reliable for medical histories or consent.
option_explanations.D: With very little English, history and consent would be unreliable.
option_explanations.E: Family interpreters still compromise accuracy and confidentiality, and delay is unnecessary when TIS is available.

key_learning_point: Limited English: use a professional interpreter (TIS National is free for GPs). Never use children, especially for sensitive topics.

subtopic: Positive iFOBT in the National Bowel Cancer Screening Program: colonoscopy, not a repeat test
stem:
A 62-year-old man sees his general practitioner in Mount Gambier, South Australia, after a letter from the National Bowel Cancer Screening Program said his immunochemical faecal occult blood test (iFOBT) was positive. He has no bowel symptoms, weight loss or family history of bowel cancer. Kits 2 and 4 years ago were negative. His abdominal and rectal examinations are normal and his haemoglobin is normal.

He asks whether he can simply repeat the test.
lead_in: Which one of the following is the most appropriate next step?

options.B: CT colonography as the first-line test
options.C: Reassure him and rescreen in 2 years
options.D: Refer for colonoscopy, ideally within 30 days
options.E: Check serum CEA

explanation_correct: A positive NBCSP iFOBT needs follow-up colonoscopy, which the program and the 2023 Australian colorectal cancer guidelines recommend should ideally occur within 30 days of the result. Repeating the iFOBT is not recommended, because bleeding from neoplasia is intermittent and a negative repeat does not cancel a positive result. A normal examination and haemoglobin do not change this.

option_explanations.A: A negative repeat does not exclude neoplasia; a positive screen needs colonoscopy.
option_explanations.B: CT colonography is for when colonoscopy is unsuitable or incomplete; colonoscopy allows biopsy and polypectomy.
option_explanations.C: A positive result needs investigation.
option_explanations.E: CEA is not a screening or diagnostic test for bowel cancer; it is used for surveillance after treatment.

key_learning_point: Positive NBCSP iFOBT: colonoscopy, ideally within 30 days. Never repeat the iFOBT to 'check' a positive.
